alalal-e79309-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 7: whether believing God, believing that God is, and believing into God are the same.

alalal-e79309-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's text 'Aliud est enim credere in Deum'.

alalal-e79309-d1e127.summary: Introduces objections that these three are unsuitably assigned to the act of faith.

alalal-e79309-d1e135.summary: First objection: one virtue relates to its object in one way, so faith does not believe God, God, and into God.

alalal-e79309-d1e144.summary: Second objection: further distinctions are possible, believing about God and toward God, so why does Lombard not distinguish faith's object by these?

alalal-e79309-d1e157.summary: Third objection: nothing tends to what is not known, and faith opens the eyes (Augustine), so faith must show the objects of all virtues, the good, the arduous, the just; Lombard's distinction of faith's object is insufficient.

alalal-e79309-d1e186.summary: Asks further how believing God, believing that God is, and believing into God differ.

alalal-e79309-d1e195.summary: Introduces arguments that they differ only materially.

alalal-e79309-d1e202.summary: First argument: believing God is believing what he says is true, and his words reveal him, so believing God terminates in believing that God is.

alalal-e79309-d1e214.summary: Second argument: Lombard wrongly makes believing into God 'loving by believing', since loving belongs to charity, not faith.

alalal-e79309-d1e227.summary: Third argument: every lover tends affectively to what it loves, so adding 'going into him by believing' to 'loving by believing' is superfluous.

alalal-e79309-d1e240.summary: Fourth argument: faith does not go but only directs the eyes to the way; hope stretches toward it and charity journeys, as Augustine suggests.

alalal-e79309-d1e251.summary: Further: adhering belongs to hope rather than faith, since it is commonly said that hope adheres and charity inheres.

alalal-e79309-d1e267.summary: Fifth argument: whoever loves and tends to God is already incorporated, so the fourth element, being incorporated into his members, was unnecessary.

alalal-e79309-d1e278.summary: Solution: believing is defined here in relation to its object, in every way the object can stand and at its best. Faith rests on first truth, taken either in a sign, an expressed infallible sign such as a word known to be God's, or in itself. Resting on it in a sign is believing God, i.e. believing the one who speaks truthfully, whether in Scripture, the heart, revelation or creatures. Resting on it in itself is either tending into it, believing into God, or assenting without tending, believing that God is. The best state of believing gathers all three: through words to God, and through God into God.
claims: Credere Deo rests on first truth in an infallible sign; credere Deum assents to it in itself; credere in Deum tends into it.
The best state of faith combines all three.
concepts: first truth in sign and in itself

alalal-e79309-d1e329.summary: Reply to the first objection: faith is one virtue with one object, first truth, and one ratio, the same truth, resting on it for its own sake; the threefold distinction concerns only accidental properties of the object, in a sign or in being, and the faith's power of tending or not tending. Charity, unlike faith, never becomes unformed, but still loves God in himself and in signs like the first goodness.
claims: The three modes of believing differ by accidental features of the one object, first truth, and by faith's power to tend toward it.

alalal-e79309-d1e366.summary: Reply to the second: the preposition 'ad' signifies end rather than object, which does not suit faith, as man is 'to the image' not the image; nor does it signify penetration of what is believed by the believer's affect.

alalal-e79309-d1e386.summary: Reply to the third: the principle that nothing tends to what is not shown to it is false throughout nature and moral virtues, which tend like nature and are more correct than any art: a heavy body falls straight to the centre without knowing geometry, and the chaste or just act without prior reasoning. The Philosopher says those brave and just without deliberation have virtue more truly. Every virtue is of itself certain of its object, and faith need not show it.
claims: Every virtue tends to its object with natural certainty, without needing faith to display it.

alalal-e79309-d1e445.summary: Reply to the first argument of the further question: the difference is not of the object's species, which would make faith several species, but of the object's properties and of the virtue's greater or lesser power.

alalal-e79309-d1e461.summary: Reply on loving by believing: no virtue alone attains beatitude, so the act of faith is defined here as faith working through love. The four elements then correspond to what is needed to attain the end: on the side of tending, love as mover and going into him as motion; on the side of union, adhering; and as consequent effect, being incorporated into his members, becoming in a way one with faith's end. In such believing, charity is not separated from faith.
claims: Credere in Deum describes faith working through love, in which charity is joined to faith.
Loving, going, adhering and incorporation correspond to the stages of attaining the end.

alalal-e79309-d1e511.summary: Reply to the third argument: going into God is not superfluous, since it differs from loving as effect from cause and motion from mover.

alalal-e79309-d1e523.summary: Reply to the fourth: faith in a way sees, and vision is outside the thing, not within, so adhering is attributed to it; hope may adhere by expectation, but cohering belongs to it rather.

alalal-e79309-d1e539.summary: Reply to the fifth: though the lover is incorporated, by nature, not time, it must first tend by love to God, who incorporates it, and adhere to him. Alternatively, the four could apply to faith's act in itself: loving as the affection for the end proper to each virtue, going as progress, adhering as union of consent, incorporation as union; but the first exposition matches Lombard's intent.

alalal-e79309.summary: Article 7 examines the triad believing God, believing that God is, and believing into God (credere Deo, Deum, in Deum), and Lombard's gloss of the last as loving by believing, going into God, adhering to him and being incorporated in his members. Albert explains that faith rests on its one object, first truth, either in an infallible sign or in itself. Resting on it in a sign, such as the word of God, is believing God. Assenting to it in itself is believing that God is. Tending into it is believing into God. The best faith unites all three. These modes differ only by accidental features of the object and by faith's power to tend, so faith remains one virtue. Credere in Deum describes faith working through love: love and going are on the side of tending, adhering on the side of union, and incorporation is the resulting effect. Against the claim that faith must show every virtue its object, Albert holds that virtues tend to their objects with natural certainty, like a falling body, without prior reasoning.
claims: Credere Deo, credere Deum and credere in Deum are three modes of relating to the one object of faith, first truth.
Credere in Deum is faith working through love, uniting faith with charity.
Virtues tend to their objects with natural certainty and need not be shown them by faith.
